title: Supervisory Toolkit for AI Use in Capital Markets (Final Report FR/02/2026)
date_evidence: Cover page: 'FR/02/2026 May 2026 Supervisory Toolkit for AI Use in Capital Markets'; IOSCO announced the final report on 25 May 2026.
key_claim: IOSCO's final supervisory toolkit covers the full lifecycle of AI from machine learning to GenAI and emerging Agentic AI; two responding members reported experiments using AI to automatically assess and oversee the performance of other AI systems ('AI as a judge'), and members raised concerns about control over systems incorporating agentic AI techniques and a need for greater focus on governance and accountability.
frame_summary: Argues securities supervisors need a practical, lifecycle toolkit to oversee firms' fast-scaling AI, flagging that agentic AI raises new control and accountability problems that existing oversight is not yet built for.
verbatim_quote: two responding IOSCO members noted experiments involving the use of AI technologies to automatically assess and oversee the performance of other AI systems ('AI as a judge'). Surveyed members indicated a need for increased focus on governance and accountability for such systems. Activities involving Agentic AI, which are typically endowed with planning capabilities, long-term memory and access to tools, are expected to have profound impact on financial products and services.
notes: Global anchor for 'AI as a judge' (AI overseeing AI) and the agentic-AI control/accountability gap.

title: FSB consults on sound practices for the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)
key_claim: The FSB published a consultation report identifying 12 sound practices for responsible AI adoption, covering organisation-wide governance (practices 1 to 4), management of AI risks across the development and deployment lifecycle (5 to 10), and cyber, ICT and third-party risks (11 to 12); it strongly encourages boards and senior management to reference them, with responses due 22 July 2026 and a final report in October 2026 as a US G20 deliverable.
frame_summary: Argues financial institutions need board-level, lifecycle governance practices to adopt AI responsibly, treating AI oversight as a senior-management accountability rather than a technical add-on.
verbatim_quote: The FSB has identified 12 sound practices to help financial institutions responsibly adopt AI. The sound practices cover organisation-wide AI governance (sound practices 1 to 4); the management and mitigation of AI risks through the different stages of AI development and deployment (sound practices 5 to 10); and the management of AI-related cyber, information and communication technology, and third-party risks (sound practices 11 and 12). The FSB strongly encourages the board and senior management of financial institutions to reference this toolkit.
notes: Global anchor: board/senior-management accountability for AI; lifecycle governance; G20 deliverable timeline.

title: Summary of AI roundtables - February 2026
key_claim: Across BoE roundtables with regulated firms, participants said the traditional model risk management approach to validation would not be sustainable as generative and agentic AI proliferated, that the emphasis on understanding a model's inner workings was not tenable for complex AI, and that the concept of a 'human-in-the-loop' was challenged by the rise of agentic AI; several suggested risk management should shift to testing, monitoring and setting guardrails around AI outcomes.
frame_summary: Argues that firms themselves see traditional model-risk validation and human-in-the-loop oversight breaking down for agentic AI, and that supervision should move toward outcome- and guardrail-based control.
verbatim_quote: firms' traditional model risk management approach to validation wouldn't be sustainable in its current form as generative AI and agentic systems proliferated. The traditional emphasis on understanding the inner workings of a model wasn't tenable or fully effective for increasingly complex AI models. The concept of having a 'human-in-the-loop' was also challenged by the rise of agentic AI. Several participants suggested that risk management needed to evolve to put greater emphasis on testing, monitoring and setting guardrails around the outcomes of broader AI systems.
notes: Primary UK anchor for the human-in-the-loop breakdown and the pivot to outcome/guardrail oversight.

title: Artificial Intelligence in the Financial System (speech by Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman, FSOC AI Roundtable)
key_claim: The Federal Reserve, with the OCC and FDIC, amended its model risk management guidance (SR letter 26-2, 17 April 2026) to clarify that it does not apply to generative or agentic AI, which now sits outside formal model-risk guidance that applies narrowly to traditional models and basic AI; Bowman said supervisors should assess whether supervisory guidance is fit for the future and that other risk-management and governance practices should support agentic AI adoption.
frame_summary: Argues US supervisors are deliberately narrowing formal model-risk rules so they no longer cover generative or agentic AI, shifting responsibility for those systems onto firms' own governance while supervisors rethink whether guidance is fit for the future.
verbatim_quote: Together with the OCC and FDIC, the Fed recently amended our model risk management guidance to clarify that it does not apply to generative or agentic AI. The revised guidance now applies narrowly to traditional models and basic AI applications. Going forward, we expect other risk-management and governance practices to support adoption of generative and agentic AI. While these supervisory tools are intended to support banks in applying sound governance and risk management, we should assess whether our supervisory guidance is fit for the future.
notes: Primary US anchor: formal model-risk guidance explicitly carves out agentic AI, creating a governance gap firms must fill.

title: From systems of record to systems of trust: A board-level playbook for governing agentic AI
key_claim: Boards are reallocating decision rights to autonomous systems while keeping governance models built for human judgement; because systems operating at machine velocity cannot be audited retroactively, boards should shift from auditing execution to governing the reward function, engineer 'legible friction' (defined pause points requiring human authorization) and accept that liability is non-transferable, citing the OECD's observation that functional frameworks for real-time agentic oversight remain absent.
frame_summary: Argues human-judgement governance models are mismatched to autonomous agents and that boards must move from controlling an agent's steps to constraining its objectives, guardrails and liability, treating governance as encoded rather than discussed.
verbatim_quote: It is reallocating decision rights to autonomous systems such as AI agents, while retaining governance models built for human judgement. Traditional compliance is often post-mortem, but systems operating at machine velocity cannot be audited retroactively. The OECD AI Policy Observatory notes that while national AI strategies proliferate, functional frameworks for real-time agentic oversight remain absent. Boards must shift from auditing execution to governing the underlying reward function.
notes: Institutional analysis: the governance-model mismatch and the move from supervising steps to governing objectives/outcomes.

title: UK Financial Services Regulators' Approach to Artificial Intelligence in 2026
key_claim: UK regulators (FCA, PRA, BoE) are keeping a technology-neutral, principles-based approach with no AI-specific rules, but firms in BoE roundtables questioned how 'human-in-the-loop' can be meaningfully applied as AI takes on more decision-making, the FCA's Mills Review asked how the Senior Managers regime operates where AI performs functions traditionally subject to human oversight, and the Treasury Committee warned that a wait-and-see approach risks serious harm.
frame_summary: Argues UK regulators are betting that existing principles and individual-accountability regimes can absorb AI, even as the human-oversight assumptions inside those regimes are openly being questioned for agentic systems.
verbatim_quote: firms raised concerns about whether traditional model risk management and validation approaches can scale effectively in the context of widespread deployment of generative and agentic AI systems. Participants also questioned how the concept of a 'human-in-the-loop' can be meaningfully applied as AI systems take on more decision-making functions.
notes: Cross-border legal analysis tying the human-oversight question to the Senior Managers regime and parliamentary pressure.

title: OCC Report Signals AI Governance Guidance Is on the Horizon as Banks Navigate Dual-Edged Risks
key_claim: The OCC's Spring 2026 Semiannual Risk Perspective supports banks' measured integration of generative and agentic AI while urging that human oversight remain embedded in workflows; the OCC, FDIC and Federal Reserve plan a request for information on model risk management as it relates to banks' use of AI, signalling formal guidance is forthcoming.
frame_summary: Argues US banking supervisors are still relying on human-oversight-in-the-workflow expectations while acknowledging their formal model-risk tools do not yet cover advanced AI, and are preparing new guidance to close the gap.
verbatim_quote: the OCC expressed support for banks' measured approach to integrating generative and agentic AI into core operational and customer service functions while maintaining guardrails and ensuring that human oversight remains embedded in workflows. the OCC, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System announced plans to issue a request for information on model risk management as it relates to banks' use of AI.
notes: US corroboration: human-oversight-in-workflow expectation plus a forthcoming RFI to close the agentic-AI guidance gap.
